steps.content:
Two Days Later
Public Security Bureau Information Desk
After your last meeting, you contacted the Public Security Bureau's Information Desk, where Murphy works. With their permission, you spend a full workday observing her at the office.
Murphy is indeed behaving a little strangely. She's constantly distracted when answering calls, unable to stay focused.

Specifically, she's destroyed one power strip by spilling water on it, leaned back too far in her chair and fallen over four times, spaced out mid-conversation and caused the caller to hang up eight times.
Her luck-altering special power hasn't disappeared. If anything, it's gotten stronger. You can feel it now, a dark cloud hanging over the entire office.
And there, right beneath the gathering clouds, sits the Goddess of Bad Luck herself, scribbling something in a notebook with a ball pen.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: What are you writing down?

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: N-nothing...
You say nothing and simply look down at her.
Within seconds, Murphy, head hung low like a guilty kitten, respectfully hands over the lined notebook with both hands.

You flip through the pages. Back in the interrogation room, you only glimpsed her notes about good luck. You didn't notice that, besides trivial everyday events, she's also been keeping track of things happening at work in detailed logs, organized by dates.
First call today: Four minutes twenty seconds in, the caller heard my joke but didn't laugh... Unlucky!
Third call today: One minute five seconds in... the caller suddenly dropped the heavy topic and started talking about her cat. Lucky!
Ninth call today: Two minutes fifteen seconds in, the conversation suddenly died, and neither of us could think of anything else to say... Unlucky!
Was suddenly craving walnuts during lunch break today. Tried cracking one twice but failed, then accidentally hurt my finger... Super unlucky! :((((
You keep turning the pages. The rest reads pretty much the same.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: These things you've been noting down...

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Huh? Wh-what about them...
She lifts her head slightly, looking at you with an anxious, insecure expression.

options: Aren't they a bit too trivial?
Are these things really worth noting down?

choices.text: Aren't they a bit too trivial?
Are these things really worth noting down?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: That entry about walnuts is at least understandable. But the ones about "the dead conversation" and "the sudden cat talk"... most people wouldn't even remember things like that. Yet not only did you record them, but you also categorized them as lucky or unlucky.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: You didn't use to obsess over these trivial things. Look, at the beginning of this notebook, you only recorded important things in your life, right? But starting from a certain point, you suddenly began logging every single detail, good or bad, no matter how minor.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: The human brain naturally filters out unimportant details. We jot down things that matter, so we don't forget. But now you're trying to care about everything. And worse, you're forcing yourself to judge if each one of them is good or bad. This will only stress you out for no reason.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Chief... So you're saying that these things I've been writing down have nothing to do with luck, and that I should just... stop judging them...

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: ...But if I stop doing this, how else am I supposed to figure out the pattern behind good luck?!

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Observation and judgment are both subjective activities. Have you ever considered that maybe this so-called <color=#fb9259>pattern</color> doesn't exist at all?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Here's what we'll do. Starting with the next call, you focus on your work, and I'll keep track of what happens during that time.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: But I won't be judging if anything is a good or bad sign, and I won't be noting down any "lucky" or "unlucky" events.
Murphy nods, tentatively accepting your idea. Once she collects herself, the Mania clouds surrounding her finally dissipate. You pull over an office chair and sit down beside her.

Over the next hour, Murphy dutifully handles one complaint call after another, while you meticulously document every detail of her conversations, matching the same level of thoroughness displayed in her own records.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Honestly, recording all this is no easy task. No wonder she was almost at a point of burnout.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Done. Take a look.
Murphy obediently sets down the receiver and takes the notebook, reading through each entry. Her expression shifts from eager anticipation to gradual disinterest, until finally, she even yawns.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: It's so... boring? They are all just trivial things that don't matter.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: That's exactly my point. Even according to your own theory, the good luck and bad luck you're experiencing now can only be considered the smallest bills in fate's currency.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Rather than desperately collecting these small bills, obsessing over their values, wanting to use them to exchange for something else...

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Why not think of them as tiny coins you're saving in a giant piggy bank? Whenever something happens, good or bad, just toss it in and don't think about it again. That way, you'll feel a lot better, and nothing will get in the way of <color=#e88490>real good luck</color> when it finally arrives.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: I mean, you've got a point, Chief...
After hearing your words, she tilts her head and slumps forward onto the desk. Her right hand picks up a ball pen and attempts to spin it, only to drop it on the desk again and again.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: But... it's just not that simple for me.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: A long time ago, I didn't use to think about my luck at all. I mean, what difference would it make? I was still the same unlucky girl anyway.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: But once I've learned that good luck really does exist, I can't help but hope for it! It's like... spending your whole life in darkness, then suddenly finding out about the sun!

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: ...Well, I'll give it a try! Stop overthinking... Yeah! I can do that!

She forces a bright smile, but the pen slips from her hand again and clatters to the floor. Scrambling to pick it up, she bumps her head on the desk as she straightens back up, letting out a soft "Ow"!
She clearly hasn't fully grasped the concept, and her agreement sounds halfhearted. Still, it's progress. You smile at the unlucky girl, watching her live up to her reputation in real time.
Ring, ring, ring!

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: ...Oh, the phone. Hello, Public Security Bureau Information Desk and Service Center!

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: Hello! Oh, yes, this voice! I remember you!

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Huh? Oh! You're the gentleman who called about the public safety concern! I remember now! You told me how unlucky you were. You always had thugs hanging around your shop while your business kept losing money...

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: Yes, yes, that's right! You fell off your chair during that call, choked on your water multiple times, and then your computer crashed, and I had to wait for it to reboot!
Not sure if it's a good thing to be remembered for those reasons... Murphy rubs her face awkwardly.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: We've already submitted the issue you reported last time. Have you encountered another problem?

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: Hahaha... Don't worry! The problem from last time hasn't been sorted out yet, but I'm only calling to thank you!

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: You want to thank me... even if it hasn't been sorted out?
Alarms blare in Murphy's head. Is this genuine gratitude a sign of good luck, or just another trap leading to bad luck?

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: After that call, I thought to myself, wow, there are people out there way unluckier than me who still manage to smile through their job. Compared to you, I suddenly realized my situation wasn't so bad after all!

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: So I just let it all go! And guess what? Barely two weeks later, I was thinking of closing my lousy shop. Then those punks showed up again. I thought to myself, to hell with it, I don't care, I'm quitting anyway!

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: So I just grabbed all that unsold junk cluttering my shop and hurled the whole pile at them!

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Huh? And did you get... beaten up by them?

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: Beaten up? No way! Some kid nearby was filming a vlog or something. He caught the moment I threw out all that stuff!

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: He edited it with some epic music and called me "the furniture store J. Chan" who taught those nasty kids a lesson. By some miracle, that video went viral!

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: All that inventory I couldn't move for three years sold out in less than half a day. Now I even have to restock every day!

steps.speaker: Grateful Citizen
steps.content: Um, hello? Did the line cut out? Anyway, just wanna say I really appreciate your help, miss. Keep up the good work. Oh, I've got a customer, gotta go!
Beep... Beep... Beep...

The call ended. Murphy remains frozen, receiver still pressed to her ear. Several seconds pass before she lowers it back into the cradle with a heavy look on her face. She turns to face you, her expression utterly deflated.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Chief, you said earlier that those events were just the normal everyday experience of the average person... that they didn't count as bad luck...

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: But even someone I've only spoken to once over the phone could tell how unlucky I am. He even used my bad luck to feel better about himself.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Fine, fine! Fate's already forsaken me anyway! He's right, I am indeed the unluckiest person in the whole world... Sob... Nobody better try to steal that title from me...
The Mania field around her begins warping again. Near the office ceiling, dark clouds of bad luck start gathering.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Well... that just set us back to square one.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: If I want to pull her out of this, I need another theory. One that can explain her bad luck in a way that's convincing, but won't make her despair. Something different from her own good luck theory...
Watching Murphy's M-value climb, you quickly usher her out of the office.
[Scene Change]
At a coffee shop outside the Public Security Bureau, you hand Murphy a hazelnut latte to help calm her down. On the table sits a collection of board games, and one in particular catches your eye.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Let's play a game about good luck and bad luck.
You pick up the somewhat worn board game and give it a little shake in Murphy's direction.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: The rules are simple. You roll the die to get your planes out. Each time you roll a six, you can launch one plane from your base. After that, you roll each turn and move your planes along the track based on the number you get.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: If your plane lands on the same spot as mine, the one that was there first gets knocked back to the base. Whoever gets all their planes to the finish point first wins. Ready?
Murphy picks up the die and nods hesitantly.
You both pick up the die and begin. Ten rounds pass. You've already launched two planes, while Murphy, who hasn't rolled a single six, can only watch helplessly as your pieces race around the board.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Chief, that's not fair! Why'd you pick a game that's all about luck? You know mine's terrible.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Look, the probability of rolling a six each turn is one in six. Now that ten rounds have passed, by that logic, the die owes you at least one plane.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: When I first started playing this game, I used to think the same way. After all, it's no fun watching everyone else's planes out on the board while yours are still stuck at home.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: But that's not how it works. A die only has six sides. It has no memory, no record of your previous rolls. No matter how many times you've failed, the odds of rolling a six next time are still just one in six.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Besides, rolling a six isn't the only outcome that matters. Launching a plane late can sometimes save you from getting knocked back. Each roll doesn't just determine a single stroke of luck, but an entire chain of <color=#fb9259>unknowns</color> you'll face afterward.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Try letting go of your resentment over the past rounds. Treat this die as the reality you're facing, and roll it again.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Let go of the resentment...
Murphy gives the die an indignant squeeze, then gently strokes it a few times to show she forgives it.

Her next rolls still aren't sixes, but your planes don't make it into the fast lane either. Murphy's planes launch over the following rounds and, by sheer coincidence, knock yours back several times. In the end, she wins the game.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Congrats on winning. Feeling any better now?

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Thank you, Chief. This is the luckiest thing that's happened to me in days.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: I didn't just invite you here to play a game. That theory of yours about good luck is like a gacha game with a pity system. You thought enough bad luck would guarantee eventual good luck. But reality is actually more like rolling a die, isn't it?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Gacha games have pity systems because someone programmed those odds. Life doesn't work like that. It's more like a die with far more sides, and it's completely out of anyone's control. No one can promise you what you'll roll next.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: The one thing I can say for certain is that your Mania can influence the die, but it won't always go the way you want. And it definitely doesn't work like a machine that follows strict rules.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Your luck hasn't changed. Your mindset has. The Murphy who was constantly unlucky was the exception. What you're dealing with now is actually closer to what normal people experience every day.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: You were used to being constantly unlucky, so days where good and bad mix together feel strange to you. That's why you insist on defining it and discovering the pattern behind it, exhausting yourself. My advice: Learn to accept your new life and adapt to it.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Accept, adapt...
Murphy fiddles with the die, repeating your words without fully understanding them.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Chief, I'm not sure I get it... but then again, maybe I do! You mean I should accept whatever result I roll, and no matter what the number is, treat it like an unknown worth looking forward to. Just like the game we were playing.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: I'm glad you've figured it out once again. I hope the "lesson" you've learned this time can last longer.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Oh, but it will! Look, Chief. To prove I mean it, I'll cross out all my old notes now!
She picks up her notebook as she speaks and starts scribbling over her previous entries, crossing out each record she's marked as good luck or bad luck.
Suddenly, her pen stops. She stares intently at one of the entries.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Cranky Old Lady... the lady who yelled at me and cost me that unlucky commendation... The last time she called was three days ago! But according to my old records, she used to call every single day...

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Why hasn't she called in so long... Did something happen to her?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: I remember you mentioned that you said something harsh to her during that last call. If I were her, I wouldn't call back either.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: ...Could this be my fault?

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Then next time she calls, I must control my temper and apologize to her. I'll explain why I acted that way last time and reflect on my own behavior... That's the right thing to do, right, Chief?

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: As long as you can stay rational and stop overthinking all that stuff about good luck, bad luck, and pity systems, I'm confident you'll handle it just fine.

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Yes, I'll definitely do my best! And thank you for everything you told me today, Chief. I'll write it all down in my notebook and commit it to memory!

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: Honestly, I still feel a little lost... But I believe everything is going in the right direction. With your help, Chief, I won't be afraid anymore!

steps.speaker: Murphy
steps.content: And that big stroke of good luck I've been waiting for so long must be on its way too!
After everything that's been said, she's still waiting for good luck?
You're still a little skeptical about her renewed understanding of luck. But at least you've seen a glimmer of hope that her understanding might still be corrected.
